definition: A temporary limitation caused by circumstances rather than a person's body, such as glare on a screen, a noisy room or holding a baby in one arm. Designs that serve permanent disabilities usually help here too.

Software or hardware people use to operate a computer in a way that suits them, such as screen readers, screen magnifiers, switch devices and voice control. It reads the page through the accessibility tree.
A simplified tree the browser builds from the DOM and CSS, where each node has a role, a name and any states or value. Assistive technologies read this tree, not the pixels on screen.
Assistive software that turns the accessibility tree into speech or braille and lets users navigate by headings, landmarks, links and form fields. Common ones are JAWS, NVDA, VoiceOver and TalkBack.
Text clipped to a 1px box with CSS so it stays in the accessibility tree but takes no visible space. Unlike display: none, screen readers still announce it.

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, the W3C standard for accessible web content. Version 2.2, published in October 2023, organises testable success criteria under four principles and three conformance levels.
The four principles at the top of WCAG: content must be Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust. Every guideline and success criterion sits under one of them.
The level at which a success criterion sits and at which conformance is claimed. Level AA, which includes all A criteria, is the target required by most laws and policies.

EU Directive 2019/882, applying since 28 June 2025, which requires covered products and services such as e-commerce, banking and ticketing to be accessible. Its reference standard, EN 301 549, maps to WCAG 2.1 AA, with a WCAG 2.2 update published in 2026.
A region of a page with a role that screen reader users can list and jump to, such as banner, navigation, main and contentinfo. HTML elements like header, nav, main and footer create them.
A value of the HTML autocomplete attribute, such as name, email or cc-number, that declares a field's purpose so browsers can fill it in. It satisfies WCAG 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose.
The text alternative of an image, given in its alt attribute. It should convey the image's purpose in context: what it shows if informative, or what it does if it is a link or button.
An image that adds no information in its context, such as a divider or an ambient photo. It gets an empty alt attribute (alt="") so screen readers skip it instead of reading its file name.
The sequence in which Tab moves through focusable elements. It follows the DOM order, so markup should match the visual reading order, and positive tabindex values should never be used.

A CSS pseudo-class that matches when the browser decides focus should be shown, such as during keyboard navigation. Styling it with a strong outline gives keyboard users a clear indicator without showing rings on mouse clicks.
A link at the very start of a page, usually hidden until focused, that jumps to the main content. It lets keyboard users bypass repeated navigation, meeting WCAG 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks.
A window that blocks the rest of the page until closed. The native dialog element opened with showModal() moves focus inside, makes the page inert, closes on Escape and restores focus afterwards.

An HTML attribute that removes an element and its descendants from focus, pointer interaction and the accessibility tree. It suits closed drawers, off-screen panels and content behind a custom overlay.

Accessible Rich Internet Applications, a set of attributes for roles, states and properties that change what the accessibility tree exposes. It never adds behaviour, so native HTML is preferred whenever it exists.
An element whose content changes are announced by screen readers without moving focus. role="status" is polite and role="alert" is assertive; the region must exist before its text changes.
A W3C guide describing common widget patterns such as tabs, disclosure, dialog and menu button, with the roles, states and keyboard interaction users expect from each.
A technique for composite widgets where only the active item has tabindex="0" and the rest have "-1". The widget is one Tab stop, and arrow keys move focus and the 0 between items.
WCAG's measure of the difference in relative luminance between two colours, from 1:1 to 21:1. Level AA needs 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text and essential non-text elements.
WCAG 1.4.10: content must fit a 320 CSS pixel wide viewport without horizontal scrolling, the width of a 1280px window at 400% zoom. Data tables and maps are exempt.
A CSS media feature that reflects the user's operating system setting for less motion. Use it to replace large animations with fades or remove them for people with vestibular disorders.
The text that identifies an element to assistive technology. Browsers compute it from aria-labelledby, then aria-label, then native labelling such as label or alt, then content, then title.
WCAG 2.5.3: when a control has visible text, its accessible name must contain that text, ideally at the start, so voice control users can activate it by saying what they see.
CSS properties such as margin-inline-start and padding-inline-end that follow the writing direction instead of physical sides, so layouts mirror automatically for right-to-left languages like Arabic.

An open-source accessibility rules engine by Deque that runs in the page and reports violations with WCAG references. It powers axe DevTools, Lighthouse's accessibility audit and test integrations such as @axe-core/playwright.
The NVDA mode in which a virtual cursor reads the page and single letters jump between elements, such as H for headings. Focus mode instead sends keys to the focused control for typing.
